title: Milan (Confessions 5–6)
hookLine: Augustine goes to hear Ambrose's style and stays for the substance

lines: HE GOES TO REVIEW THE BISHOP.
cards: A job offer. The city of Milan needs a teacher of public speaking, and Augustine gets the post. He's a professional now: he teaches young men how to persuade a room.

He arrives in Milan and, as part of settling in, goes to meet the bishop. It's Ambrose, the governor the crowd made bishop, the one who wrote to the emperor. Augustine has heard Ambrose is a superb speaker.
So when Ambrose preaches, he goes to church. Not to pray. To review the performance.

teach.b: Augustine tells it in Books Five and Six of the Confessions. First, the welcome.
Ambrose received him like a father, and Augustine began to love him, not yet as a teacher of truth, he admits, just as a man who was kind to him. Then the sermons.
Augustine sits there like a critic. Is the bishop as good as his reputation? He listens closely to the words and doesn't care about the content.
He even enjoys the sweetness of the speaking. And then something happens he didn't plan.

teach.h: THE TRUTH CAME IN WITH THE WORDS.
teach.b: While he was opening his ears to how well Ambrose spoke, he says, how truly he spoke came in along with it, little by little. He couldn't separate the two. He came for the style, and the substance got in.
One thing that got in was a way of reading the Old Testament. Augustine had found some of its stories crude. Ambrose kept repeating a line from Saint Paul.
In the Douay-Rheims: "the letter killeth, but the spirit quickeneth." Read for the spirit, and the hard passages opened up. And one more picture from Milan: Ambrose reading.

His eyes moved over the page, his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were still. Augustine and his friends would come in, find him reading silently, sit a while without disturbing him, and leave.
He wanted to talk to the bishop and couldn't get the time. He got the sermons instead.

how: At Mass the homily follows the Gospel, and the priest or deacon explains the readings; Catholics who want more may join a Bible study or read with the help of the Church's commentaries.

games.why: Augustine says that while he listened for how well Ambrose spoke, how truly he spoke came in too, little by little.

practice: Think of a voice you hear often, a preacher, a coworker, a relative, someone online, whose style dazzles you or grates on you.
Set the style aside, say one thing they said lately back to yourself in plain, flat words, and ask whether any of it is true.
